The Means

AlgebraLimitsFractions
Game: Find the middle of a set of numbers in many ways. The green bar is the mean, and the exponent decides which kind of mean it is.
How to play: Drag the purple bars up and down, or use the arrow keys on a focused bar. Slide the exponent: 1 adds, 0 multiplies, minus 1 flips. Change the size of the set below.

Look for the math

If a car drives for one hour at 20 miles per hour and another hour at 30, its average speed is 25: the arithmetic mean. If instead it drives half the distance at each speed, the average is 24, not 25: the harmonic mean. The same rule, distance divided by time, is applied to different things. Both answers are checked in the test (25 and 24, and 2d ÷ (d/20 + d/30) = 24).

One formula for all the means

For positive numbers a₁ … aₙ and an exponent r, the mean is Mr = ((a₁r + … + aₙr) / n)1/r. With r = 1 it is the arithmetic mean, with r = −1 the harmonic mean (and H(a) = 1 / A(1/a), which the test confirms), and with r = 2 the quadratic mean. At r = 0 the formula breaks, but the means settle down to the geometric mean (a₁ ⋯ aₙ)1/n as r goes to 0, so that is what the page shows at 0. The test compares M at r = ±0.0001 with it on thousands of sets.

The means line up

Slide the exponent from −50 to 50 and the green bar only ever rises. This is the power mean inequality: Mr ≥ Mr/2 for r > 0, which comes from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and from it the famous arithmetic ≥ geometric ≥ harmonic. The test checked all of this at every exponent from −50 to 50 on 5,000 random sets of 2 to 30 numbers. All the means are equal only when all the numbers are equal.

The two ends

For very negative r the mean hugs the smallest number and for very large r the largest. At r = ±50 it is within a factor n1/50 of the end, which the test confirms.

Make all the bars equal. What happens to the means? Then make one bar much taller than the others and slide the exponent from −50 to 50.
